title: Counting it loss (Philippians 3:1–11)
hook: everything Paul was proud of, he counts as loss compared with knowing Christ

segments.voice: Yesterday, Timothy and Epaphroditus, the two helpers Paul named, and your line was hold such in honor. Whose name did you say out loud? Day six hundred sixty-three.

A résumé, printed on the good paper, in the right fonts. Born into the right family. Top schools. The best teachers. A record nobody can fault. Then the owner takes a red pen and writes across the whole page, in big letters: loss. Not shredding it. Not lying about it. Just marking it down, as if the numbers had been in the wrong column the whole time. That is close to what Paul does in the third chapter of Philippians. He lays out every credential he ever had, one by one, and then moves the whole list from one side of the ledger to the other.

Here's the list, in the King James Bible: "Circumcised the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, an Hebrew of the Hebrews; as touching the law, a Pharisee." Every item is something to be proud of. He kept the law of his people with great zeal, and says that by its measure of righteousness he was blameless. Notice he is not mocking any of it. These are real goods, an honored family, a faithful upbringing, a serious life. That's what makes the next line land. "But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ." It's bookkeeping language. Gain and loss, profit and debit. Then he goes further: "I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord." All things. And he uses a rough word for them, one that means refuse, the scraps you throw out. Older English Bibles put it bluntly as dung. Why so strong? Because, Paul says, what he wants now is not a record but a person: "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings." Know, here, is not knowing about. It's the way you know a friend. Christians read this passage in different ways. Some hear a conversion from one way of standing before God to another. Others stress that Paul never stops being a Jew, and that what he counts as loss is his own standing, his pride, not the Torah or his people. Both readings see the turn: the things that once defined him no longer get to.
screen: then, large: `I COUNT ALL THINGS BUT LOSS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one pride. Settle, and breathe. Name something you're proud of that quietly runs your life. A title. A grade. Being the one who's always right, or always busy, or always fine. Don't throw it away. It may be a real good, as Paul's were. Just picture writing it on a card and moving it across the table, out of the center. Notice what's left in the middle when it's gone. Notice if your shoulders change. If you pray, you can hand it to God and leave the card there. The bell holds the time.
Counting it loss. Paul's bookkeeping turn: every credential he had, moved to the loss column, compared with knowing Christ.
Your line: all else is loss. Today, when the urge comes to mention your credentials, skip it once, and see whether the conversation is any worse. Day six hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Many Christians read Philippians 3 when thinking about pride and identity, and some churches use verses 7 to 11 in Lent as a reflection on what to set aside.

fork.setup: you're Paul. you have the family, the training and a spotless record. what do you do with it?
options: lead with it, so people trust you.
count it all as loss compared with knowing Christ.
fork.reveal: "what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ." he doesn't hide the list. he re-files it.

original.note: Greek: loss, damage, a business write-off. Paul uses it in verses 7 and 8.

trapdoor: what you thought: Paul saying his past was bad.
what it means: his real goods, family, law, zeal, re-counted as loss beside knowing Christ.
what a scholar hears: gain and loss are ledger words; some scholars today read the loss as Paul's own standing and pride, not a rejection of his people or the Torah.

notes: Greek σκύβαλα (3:8): refuse, scraps, sometimes dung; the KJV has 'dung'. Confirm the gloss.
ζημία appears in 3:7 and 3:8 (with the related verb ἐζημιώθην in 3:8). Confirm.

The two readings (conversion of standing; the 'new perspective' stress that Paul remains a Jew and counts his own standing as loss) are given without ranking. Confirm fairness to Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox readers and to Jewish listeners.
